headline: Japan's Digital-Twin Commission Preempted a Commercial Three.js Sky System
lede: Dan Greenheck, a Three.js educator who sells commercial WebGL add-ons, was midway through building Three.js Sky Pro — a paid atmosphere-and-clouds package — when he discovered that a Tokyo design consultancy had already released the same thing, more capable, under an MIT licence, for free. The library is @takram/three-geospatial, and its existence is almost perfectly ironic: it is a side effect of a Japanese government contract, published when that engagement ended.
body:
Greenheck had established proof of market with **Three.js Water Pro**, a physically-based ocean shader he sells through threejsroadmap.com. Sky Pro was to be the sequel: a complete real-time sky system covering volumetric clouds, dynamic atmosphere, and physically accurate lighting, packaged cleanly and priced accordingly. The strategy mirrors a pattern familiar from game-engine asset stores — find a technically hard sub-problem, absorb the physics and tuning work, and charge for the convenience of not having to do it yourself.

**@takram/three-geospatial** is a monorepo of packages built by Takram, a Tokyo design-and-engineering consultancy, as the rendering layer for PLATEAU VIEW 3.0, a national digital-twin city platform commissioned by Japan's Cabinet Office under its *SBIR* program. The client was Eukarya; the goal was a browser-based system for streaming and rendering photorealistic 3D city data for urban planning and government visualization. When Takram's engagement concluded in March 2025, the team published the entire codebase under MIT. The primary author, Shota Matsuda, is a design engineer at the firm. The library had accumulated 1,400 GitHub stars by mid-2026.

The atmosphere package implements Eric Bruneton's *precomputed atmospheric scattering*: the physics of sunlight interacting with air molecules — Rayleigh scattering from nitrogen and oxygen, Mie scattering from aerosols, ozone absorption — are pre-baked into lookup textures at load time, so sky colour, aerial perspective, and ground illumination can be sampled cheaply at runtime. The clouds package adds *volumetric rendering* via *ray marching* — stepping a virtual ray through a 3D density field and accumulating scattered and absorbed light — plus *Beer Shadow Maps*, a technique that lets clouds cast physically plausible soft shadows on terrain and buildings below. A *temporal upscaling* pass reconstructs full-resolution frames from one-sixteenth of the ray-marching work per frame, a budget trick borrowed from temporal anti-aliasing. The live demo visible in the tweet screenshot shows all of this running over London's photorealistic *3D Tiles* geometry, streamed from Google (GOOGL).

The episode illustrates an asymmetry that haunts commercial add-on markets for open-source 3D frameworks. Three.js is community-maintained; its ecosystem — including *React Three Fiber* (R3F), the React abstraction layer for Three.js, and *drei*, a large library of reusable R3F helper components — is overwhelmingly free. A commercial vendor building atop it competes not just with other vendors but with the accumulated output of government contracts, research labs, and corporate open-source publications, none of which are priced to undercut anyone. In this case the competition was structural: Takram's work existed to be demonstrated to a government client, and once the demonstration was done, publication cost nothing.

Greenheck's own account of the miss is instructive: he had searched for prior art and failed to find it, likely because the library's name — geospatial, not sky or atmosphere — does not map naturally onto the vocabulary a Three.js developer uses when looking for a sky system. The search failure is a small, common story about how the open-source commons get filled from unexpected directions: procurement programs, client work, academic prototypes, research lab drops — at a rate no single developer can fully track.

concepts.definition: A rendering technique, formalized by Eric Bruneton, that pre-bakes the physics of light moving through the atmosphere into lookup textures at load time. At runtime the shader samples these tables instead of computing expensive integrals on the fly, making physically accurate sky colour, aerial perspective, and sun/moon lighting affordable on consumer GPUs.

A rendering technique in which a virtual ray is stepped forward through a 3D volume — such as a cloud density field — in small increments. At each step the algorithm accumulates how much light is scattered toward the camera or absorbed, producing soft volumetric effects impossible to achieve with traditional polygon rendering.

A shadow-mapping method adapted for volumetric media. Instead of storing a simple depth value per texel, the map encodes how much light is absorbed as it passes through a cloud volume, allowing clouds to cast physically plausible, soft shadows on terrain and buildings below rather than hard geometric outlines.

A performance technique in which only a fraction of final-resolution pixels are computed each frame, and the missing pixels are reconstructed by accumulating information from prior frames. Used here to make expensive ray-marched cloud rendering affordable in real time; related to TAA (Temporal Anti-Aliasing) and commercial upscalers such as DLSS.

A family of rendering techniques for objects that have internal density rather than a hard surface — clouds, fog, smoke, fire. Unlike polygon rendering, volumetric methods simulate how light scatters and is absorbed as it travels through a participating medium.

An open standard from Cesium (now ratified by the OGC) for streaming large-scale 3D geospatial content — photogrammetric building meshes, terrain, point clouds — over the web. Google Maps Platform distributes Photorealistic 3D Tiles of major cities using this format, enabling browser-based city rendering without pre-downloading entire datasets.

Small Business Innovation Research — a competitive grant and contract programme used by governments to fund applied R&D by private companies. Japan's Cabinet Office SBIR funded the Eukarya/Takram engagement that produced the three-geospatial library. The United States runs a parallel programme through federal agencies.

A React renderer for Three.js maintained by the Poimandres open-source collective. It lets developers describe 3D scenes as React component trees, making Three.js objects reactive to application state. The @takram/three-geospatial packages ship native R3F components alongside plain Three.js classes.

A large, free collection of reusable React Three Fiber helper components — camera controls, loaders, shaders, environment maps, and more — maintained by the Poimandres collective and distributed under MIT. It is the dominant convenience library in the R3F ecosystem.

repos.summary: A monorepo of MIT-licensed Three.js libraries for geospatial rendering, covering precomputed atmospheric scattering, volumetric cloud rendering with Beer Shadow Maps, geospatial coordinate utilities, and post-processing effects. Built by Takram as the rendering engine for Japan's PLATEAU VIEW 3.0 digital-twin platform, then open-sourced when the engagement concluded in March 2025. Integrates natively with React Three Fiber and the 3DTilesRendererJS streaming library.
